subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 9-year-old girl presents with 5 days of fever and joint pain. Three weeks ago she had a sore throat that was never treated. Examination shows painful swelling of her knees and ankles that appears to move from joint to joint over several days, and a new blowing holosystolic murmur at the apex. Anti-streptolysin O (ASO) titers are elevated.
question: Which of the following additional findings would satisfy another major (JONES) criterion for this patient's suspected condition?

options.text: Painful, raised, violaceous nodules on the pads of her fingers
Linear hemorrhages beneath the fingernails
An evanescent rash with erythematous rings and central clearing on the trunk
Painless, flat, erythematous macules on the palms and soles
Retinal hemorrhages with pale centers on fundoscopy

explanation_correct: This child has acute rheumatic fever after untreated group A streptococcal pharyngitis, evidenced by the migratory polyarthritis (Joint) and new mitral murmur (carditis), the two criteria already present. An evanescent rash with erythematous rings and central clearing is erythema marginatum, another major (JONES) criterion. The mnemonic J♥NES comprises migratory polyarthritis, pancarditis, subcutaneous nodules, erythema marginatum, and Sydenham chorea.

explanation_incorrect.A: Painful, raised, violaceous nodules on finger pads are Osler nodes, a feature of infective endocarditis; the rheumatic fever criterion is painless subcutaneous nodules over extensor surfaces.
explanation_incorrect.B: Splinter hemorrhages (linear hemorrhages beneath the nails) are vascular phenomena of infective endocarditis and are not part of the Jones major criteria for rheumatic fever.
explanation_incorrect.D: Painless, flat, erythematous macules on the palms and soles are Janeway lesions of infective endocarditis, a different disease that also causes fever and a new murmur but follows bacteremia rather than streptococcal pharyngitis.
explanation_incorrect.E: Retinal hemorrhages with pale centers (Roth spots) are immunologic phenomena of infective endocarditis, not a Jones major criterion.

educationalObjective: The major Jones criteria for rheumatic fever are J♥NES: migratory polyarthritis, pancarditis, subcutaneous nodules, erythema marginatum, and Sydenham chorea.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 10-year-old boy is diagnosed with acute rheumatic fever 3 weeks after untreated group A streptococcal pharyngitis. An endomyocardial biopsy shows interstitial granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells and enlarged macrophages with ovoid, wavy, rodlike nuclei. Anti-DNase B titers are elevated.
question: Which of the following best describes the pathogenesis of this patient's cardiac findings?

options.text: Direct invasion of the myocardium by streptococci with toxin-mediated myocyte lysis
Deposition of circulating antigen-antibody complexes in the myocardium (type III hypersensitivity)
Cytotoxic T lymphocyte–mediated killing of myocytes infected by the bacteria
Antibodies against streptococcal M protein cross-reacting with cardiac myosin (type II hypersensitivity)
IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation in the pericardium

explanation_correct: Rheumatic fever is an immune-mediated (type II hypersensitivity) disease, not a direct effect of bacteria: antibodies generated against the M protein of group A streptococci cross-react with self antigens, often cardiac myosin — molecular mimicry. The biopsy findings support this: Aschoff bodies (granulomas with giant cells) and Anitschkow cells (enlarged macrophages with ovoid, wavy, rodlike nuclei) are the characteristic histology, with elevated anti-streptolysin O and anti-DNase B titers confirming prior streptococcal pharyngeal infection.

explanation_incorrect.A: Rheumatic fever is explicitly not a direct effect of the bacteria; group A streptococci do not invade and lyse myocardial cells, and the disease is a nonsuppurative sequela occurring weeks after the pharyngitis.
explanation_incorrect.B: Type III immune complex deposition characterizes diseases such as glomerulonephritis and the immunologic phenomena of endocarditis; rheumatic fever is a type II antibody-mediated cross-reactive process, not immune complex deposition.
explanation_incorrect.C: Cytotoxic T cell killing applies to virally infected cells, but this boy's myocytes are not infected — the injury is antibody-mediated molecular mimicry against myosin.
explanation_incorrect.E: IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation is type I hypersensitivity (allergy/anaphylaxis) and has no role in rheumatic carditis, which is antibody-mediated type II hypersensitivity.

educationalObjective: Rheumatic fever is a type II hypersensitivity disease in which antibodies to streptococcal M protein cross-react with cardiac myosin (molecular mimicry), producing Aschoff bodies and Anitschkow cells.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 42-year-old woman from an area with limited access to medical care is evaluated for gradually worsening exertional dyspnea and occasional hemoptysis. She had rheumatic fever twice during childhood. Examination shows a loud S1, an opening snap, and a low-pitched diastolic rumble at the apex best heard with the bell in the left lateral decubitus position.
question: Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's murmur?

options.text: Mitral stenosis from leaflet thickening and fusion following prior rheumatic inflammation
Mitral regurgitation from acute rheumatic valvulitis
Aortic regurgitation from dilation of the aortic root and valve ring
Tricuspid stenosis from rheumatic involvement of a low-pressure valve
A left atrial myxoma causing intermittent "ball valve" obstruction

explanation_correct: Rheumatic heart disease most commonly affects the mitral valve (mitral > aortic >> tricuspid, because high-pressure valves are affected most). Early disease causes valvular regurgitation, while late disease — decades after recurrent rheumatic fever, as in this patient — produces stenosis from leaflet thickening, fusion, and calcification. The combination of a loud S1, opening snap, and low-pitched diastolic rumble at the apex is the classic auscultatory triad of mitral stenosis.

explanation_incorrect.B: Mitral regurgitation is the early valvular lesion of rheumatic carditis and produces a holosystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla, not the diastolic rumble with opening snap heard here.
explanation_incorrect.C: Aortic regurgitation from root and valve ring dilation is the classic lesion of syphilitic aortitis in tertiary syphilis, and it produces an early diastolic decrescendo murmur along the left sternal border rather than an apical rumble.
explanation_incorrect.D: Tricuspid valve involvement in rheumatic heart disease is much less common (mitral > aortic >> tricuspid) because lower-pressure valves are affected less, and tricuspid stenosis would produce a rumble at the lower left sternal border that increases with inspiration.
explanation_incorrect.E: An atrial myxoma can mimic mitral stenosis with a diastolic "tumor plop," but this patient's documented recurrent rheumatic fever and the presence of an opening snap with a loud S1 point to rheumatic mitral stenosis, the far more common cause.

educationalObjective: Rheumatic heart disease affects the mitral valve most often (mitral > aortic >> tricuspid) and causes early regurgitation but late stenosis, classically mitral stenosis with an opening snap and apical diastolic rumble.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 30-year-old man with severe mitral stenosis undergoes mitral valve replacement. Histologic examination of the resected left atrial appendage shows interstitial granulomas with multinucleated giant cells and enlarged macrophages with ovoid, wavy, rodlike nuclei. He recalls recurrent throat infections during childhood but no skin infections, and serology from that period showed elevated anti-DNase B titers.
question: Which of the following preceding infections is most likely responsible for these histologic findings?

options.text: Viridans streptococcal bacteremia following a dental procedure
Group A streptococcal cellulitis of the leg
Coxsackievirus B infection
Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia
Untreated group A streptococcal pharyngitis

explanation_correct: The granulomas with giant cells are Aschoff bodies and the macrophages with ovoid, wavy, rodlike nuclei are Anitschkow cells, the characteristic histology of rheumatic heart disease. Rheumatic fever is a nonsuppurative consequence specifically of PHARYNGEAL infection with group A β-hemolytic streptococci — the childhood recurrent throat infections with elevated anti-DNase B titers in this vignette. Notably, group A streptococcal skin infections do not cause rheumatic fever, making the pharyngeal localization a key test point.

explanation_incorrect.A: Viridans streptococcal bacteremia after dental procedures causes subacute infective endocarditis, which produces friable vegetations on damaged valves, not Aschoff bodies or Anitschkow cells.
explanation_incorrect.B: This is the key trap: group A streptococcal skin infections (eg, cellulitis, impetigo) do not lead to rheumatic fever; only pharyngeal infection does, and this patient's history specifically documents recurrent throat infections.
explanation_incorrect.C: Coxsackievirus B causes viral myocarditis with a lymphocytic infiltrate and focal myocyte necrosis, a diffuse inflammatory process rather than granulomatous Aschoff bodies.
explanation_incorrect.D: Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia causes acute infective endocarditis with large, destructive vegetations on previously normal valves, not the granulomatous lesions of rheumatic carditis.

educationalObjective: Rheumatic fever is a nonsuppurative sequela specifically of group A streptococcal pharyngeal (not skin) infection, and its histologic hallmarks are Aschoff bodies and Anitschkow cells.
